segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: Section 1: Social Dialogue

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: Hi, I'm calling about the archive digitisation project. I'm a postgraduate student in history, and I'd like to know if I can access some of the digitised materials for my dissertation.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: Of course. Can I take your name and student number first?

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: Yes, it's Daniel Foster, and my student number is 2045783.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: Thank you, Daniel. So, which collections are you interested in?

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: I'm particularly interested in the papers of the first Vice-Chancellor, Sir John Marston. I understand they've been digitised.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: Yes, they have. The Marston papers were part of the first phase of the project. But I should mention that some items are restricted due to data protection. The personal correspondence from the 1920s is available, but the medical records are not.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: That's fine. I'm mainly interested in his correspondence about the university's founding.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: Good. You can access the digitised images through our online catalogue. You'll need to create an account first. Have you used the catalogue before?

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: No, I haven't. Is it complicated?

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: Not really. You just need to register with your university email address, and then you can search by name, date, or subject. You can also download images for personal research use, but you can't publish them without permission.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: I see. And is there a limit on how many images I can download?

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: Yes, there is a limit of 200 images per month for postgraduate students. If you need more, you can apply for an extension.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: OK, that should be enough for now. One more thing: can I visit the archive in person to see the originals?

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: Yes, you can. The reading room is open Monday to Friday, from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. You'll need to book an appointment at least two days in advance. And you'll need to bring your student card.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: Great. Thank you for your help.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: You're welcome. Good luck with your dissertation.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: Section 2: Social Monologue

segments.speaker: Speaker
segments.text: Welcome to the Northfield University Archive. This short guide will tell you what you need to know before your first visit. The archive is located in the Hartley Building, which is on the eastern edge of the campus, next to the botanical gardens. If you're coming by bus, take the number 14 or the number 22 and get off at the stop called 'University East'. From there, it's a five-minute walk.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: When you arrive, please come to the reception desk on the ground floor. You'll be asked to sign in and show some form of identification. A student card or a driving licence is fine. You'll also be asked to leave your coat and bag in a locker, which is free of charge. You can bring a pencil and paper into the reading room, but pens are not allowed, and you cannot bring food or drink.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: The reading room is on the first floor. It has space for up to twenty researchers at a time. You don't need to book a seat, but if you want to use one of the specialist scanners, you should reserve it in advance. The scanners are free to use, but there is a charge for printing: ten pence per page for black and white, and twenty pence for colour.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: If you need help finding materials, please ask a member of staff. We're always happy to help, but we're a small team, so please be patient during busy periods. The archive is usually busiest in the mornings, so if you prefer a quieter environment, come in the afternoon.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: Finally, a word about handling documents. You must wash your hands before handling any original material, and you should use the foam supports provided for bound volumes. Never place a document flat on the desk without support, and never write on top of a document. If you notice any damage, please report it to a member of staff immediately. We want to preserve these materials for future generations, and your cooperation is essential.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: Thank you for listening, and we look forward to welcoming you to the archive.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: Section 3: Academic Discussion

segments.speaker: Tutor
segments.text: OK, let's begin. Today we're going to discuss the case study of the Northfield Archive Digitisation Project. I'd like you to think about the challenges the project faced and what lessons can be drawn. Maria, what struck you most about the project?

segments.speaker: Maria
segments.text: I think the most interesting thing was the metadata issue. The project team estimated that cataloguing would take about 20% of the time, but it actually took nearly 40%. That's a huge difference.

segments.speaker: Tutor
segments.text: Yes, that's a good point. Why do you think they underestimated it?

segments.speaker: Maria
segments.text: Well, the text says the existing catalogue was incomplete and sometimes inaccurate. So the metadata specialist had to check each item against other sources. That must have been very time-consuming.

segments.speaker: Tutor
segments.text: Exactly. And what about the selection process? James, you looked at that, didn't you?

segments.speaker: James
segments.text: Yes. I found it interesting that the selection was controversial. Some users complained that their favourite collections were being ignored. But the project team argued that the selection was based on clear criteria.

segments.speaker: Tutor
segments.text: What were those criteria?

segments.speaker: James
segments.text: They prioritised items that were both fragile and in high demand. So some popular but robust items were deferred, and some fragile but rarely requested items were included because of their preservation needs.

segments.speaker: Tutor
segments.text: Good. Now, what about the impact of the pandemic?

segments.speaker: Maria
segments.text: The project was delayed by about six months because imaging work couldn't be done remotely. That seems like a significant setback.

segments.speaker: Tutor
segments.text: Yes, but did the project still achieve its objectives?

segments.speaker: James
segments.text: Mostly. By the end of 2021, over 11,000 items had been digitised, which was about 92% of the target. And the online catalogue was launched in October 2021.

segments.speaker: Tutor
segments.text: So would you say the project was a success?

segments.speaker: Maria
segments.text: I think so, but with some caveats. The metadata took longer than expected, and two items had to be excluded because of copyright issues. So there were some failures.

segments.speaker: Tutor
segments.text: That's a balanced view. Now, let's think about the lessons for future projects. What would you do differently?

segments.speaker: James
segments.text: I would plan more time for metadata and copyright clearance from the beginning. The project manager said that was a key lesson.

segments.speaker: Maria
segments.text: I agree. And I think it's important to involve the conservator at every stage, not just at the beginning. The case study mentions that the conservator was involved throughout.

segments.speaker: Tutor
segments.text: Good. Let's move on to consider how these lessons might apply to the second phase of the project.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: Section 4: Academic Lecture

segments.speaker: Lecturer
segments.text: Good morning. Today's lecture is about the principles of digitisation, and I'll be drawing on the case study of the Northfield Archive Digitisation Project, which you should have read about. I want to focus on four key areas: selection, imaging, metadata, and preservation. These are the four pillars of any digitisation project, and if any one of them is weak, the whole project suffers.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: Let's start with selection. Selection is often seen as a simple matter of choosing what to digitise, but in practice it's a complex balancing act. You have to consider the fragility of the original, the demand from users, and the legal restrictions. Sometimes these factors conflict. For example, a document might be extremely fragile and therefore a high priority for preservation, but if it's also subject to copyright, you may not be able to put it online. So you have to make difficult choices. The Northfield project prioritised items that were both fragile and in high demand, but even that criterion led to complaints from some users.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: Next, imaging. The quality of the digital image is crucial. A low-resolution scan might be fine for someone who just wants to read the text, but it won't be adequate for a researcher who needs to examine handwriting or paper texture. So imaging standards must be matched to the purpose of the project. High-end projects may use specialised equipment, but smaller projects can use good-quality digital cameras. What matters most is consistency and careful handling of the original.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: Now, metadata. This is the information that describes the image: who created the document, when, what it's about, and so on. Without metadata, a digital image is almost useless because no one can find it. Metadata creation is often the most time-consuming part of a project, and it's frequently underestimated. In the Northfield project, metadata took nearly 40% of the time, compared with an estimate of 20%. That's a valuable lesson.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: Finally, preservation. This applies to both the original and the digital file. The original must be protected during scanning, and the digital file must be preserved for the long term. Digital storage is not permanent: files can become corrupted, formats can become obsolete, and storage media can fail. So you need a digital preservation plan, including backups and regular checks.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: To conclude, digitisation is not just about taking photographs. It's about creating a resource that people can actually use. And that requires careful planning in all four areas. Thank you. I'll take questions now.
